sections.h2: Where do I search Cameron County property records?
sections.html:
Start with the Official Public Records search linked from the Cameron County Clerk's page, then call the Brownsville main office at (956) 544-0815 about anything the search does not show. The clerk's Recordings Division files and keeps real property records, personal property records, notices of trustee sales and public notices. Records that no law or court order restricts are open through the Public Records Search.

The clerk's public access portals page lists separate databases for foreclosure sales, official records, official records from 1848 to 1912, and judicial records. A very old instrument belongs in the 1848 to 1912 portal, so check there before you decide a record is missing.

sections.h2: Which Cameron County Clerk office should I visit?
sections.html:
Go to the Brownsville main office at 835 East Levee Street, 3rd Floor, for deeds and liens. The clerk lists four more locations, and the one nearest your house may save a trip.

  • Older civil, probate and deed volumes are stored at the records management facility in the San Benito annex building.

sections.h2: How do I record a deed in Cameron County?
sections.html:
Bring the original deed with original signatures, because the clerk will not record a copy. File it at the Brownsville office or any satellite office, or mail it to the Filing and Recording Department, P.O. Box 2178, Brownsville, TX 78522.

The clerk says recordings are completed as they arrive. Once a document is cashiered, given an instrument number and scanned, the original goes back to the filer. Electronic filing runs through the e-recording companies the clerk names, and the page limits it to groups such as Texas attorneys, banks, credit unions and title insurance companies or agents.

Two state rules decide whether the clerk can accept your deed. It has to be acknowledged before a notary or another authorized officer, or sworn before two witnesses, under Property Code 12.001(b). And a missing grantee mailing address can add a $25 charge, according to the Texas county clerk manual.

On price, the clerk's land records page prints $35 for the first page and $4 for each added page, in its paragraph on recording a release of lien. The state manual lists a $5 first page and $4 for each added page as the base recording fee, before add-on records fees. Ask the clerk which total applies to your deed before you mail a check, and make it payable to the Cameron County Clerk.

sections.h2: How do I get a copy of a recorded deed or check for liens?
sections.html:
Use the Official Public Records Search, choose Property Records, and pull a plain or certified copy there. You can also email officialpublicrecords@co.cameron.tx.us. For a certified copy by mail, write to the County Clerk's Office, P.O. Box 2178, Brownsville, TX 78522-2178. The printed charge is $1 per page, $5 per certification and $5 per search.

Liens recorded against a property show up in the same search. The clerk states that its office does not guarantee a clear title and is not responsible for encumbrances, and it points owners to title companies and attorneys. For a sale, the title company will look for:

  • Deeds of trust and the releases that should follow a payoff
  • Tax liens and judgments filed against the owner
  • Probate filings when an owner has died
  • Gaps in the chain of deeds, such as a missing heir's signature

sections.h2: Does the Cameron Appraisal District keep deeds or tax bills?
sections.html:
No. The Cameron Appraisal District sets values and administers exemptions, and its own site sends deed copy and subdivision plat requests to the county clerk. It also says it does not collect taxes or hold tax amounts.

The district notes that people often mistake it for the Cameron County Tax Office, which sits across U.S. Highway 83 at 1390 W Expressway 83 in San Benito. The district opens at 7:30 and closes at 5:30 from Monday through Thursday, and keeps 8 to 5 on Fridays. Property Search and Map Search are linked from its home page.

The Texas Comptroller calendar fixes value and ownership as of January 1. Owners can protest by May 15 or the 30th day after the appraisal notice, whichever is later, and the payment page says a bill unpaid on February 1 turns delinquent. School districts must give a $140,000 homestead exemption, and the application goes to the appraisal district.

sections.h2: What if a Cameron County owner died and the title is unclear?
sections.html:
A probate filing usually clears it. The clerk's Probate Department, at 974 East Harrison Street, 2nd Floor, Brownsville, handles probate of a will and issuance of letters testamentary, probate of a will as a muniment of title, letters of administration and determination of heirship.

The department also describes a small estate affidavit. By the clerk's description it applies when there is no will, the estate is under $75,000 and no real estate is involved. A house therefore needs one of the other routes. Call (956) 544-0826 for forms, and ask the clerk for the 2026 probate fee schedule that the department page links.

sections.h2: What do the Census figures say about Cameron County housing?
sections.html:
The county covers a large area and holds a few hundred thousand people. These figures come from Census QuickFacts:

  • Population: 433,946 in the July 2025 estimate, up from 421,017 at the 2020 census
  • Land area: 891.71 square miles, about 472 people per square mile in 2020
  • Housing units: 166,569 in July 2025, with 2,702 building permits in 2025
  • Owner-occupied rate: 65.2%, and 138,433 households
  • Home value reported by owners, middle figure: $136,500 (2020 to 2024)
  • Middle gross rent: $912, and middle household income: $52,601

These are county-wide medians. A house in Brownsville, Harlingen or San Benito can sit far above or below them, so use the figures as background only.

sections.h2: When and where are Cameron County foreclosure sales held?
sections.html:
The clerk's page says the sale runs on the first Tuesday of every month between 10:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m., on the west side of the Cameron County Courthouse or at another spot the Commissioners Court designates. The sale is open to the public for bidding, and the notices are filed with the clerk's Recordings Division.

The same page prints redemption periods: two years for agricultural-use or homestead property and six months for all other property, counted from the date the deed is recorded. Questions about tax certificates go to the Tax Assessor-Collector at 956-544-0800. If your house has a notice of sale on file, tell a title company early, because it affects what can still be recorded and sold.

faqs.q: Where is the Cameron County Clerk's main office?
faqs.a: It is at 835 East Levee Street, 3rd Floor, Brownsville, TX 78520, and the phone is (956) 544-0815. The clerk also lists offices in San Benito, Harlingen and La Feria, plus a courthouse location at 974 E. Harrison Street.

faqs.q: Will the Cameron County Clerk record a photocopy of my deed?
faqs.a: No. The clerk's land records page says the original documents with original signatures are required and that the office will not record a copy. After scanning, the original is returned to the filer.

faqs.q: What does a certified copy of a deed cost in Cameron County?
faqs.a: By mail, the clerk prints $1 per page, $5 per certification and $5 per search. Plain and certified copies can also be requested through the Official Public Records Search under Property Records.

faqs.q: Can the Cameron Appraisal District give me a copy of my deed?
faqs.a: No. The district's site says it does not give out copies of deeds or subdivision plats and refers those requests to the Cameron County Clerk's office. Call the clerk at (956) 544-0815.

faqs.q: How can I tell if my Cameron County house is facing a foreclosure sale?
faqs.a: Search the clerk's foreclosure sales portal and the Official Public Records for a notice of trustee sale. Sales take place on the first Tuesday of each month, so a notice on file points to the next first Tuesday. A title company can confirm the status.
